procedural_history.originating_court: Industrial Tribunal, Delhi (Sri Ram Kanwar, Industrial Tribunal)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated April 17, 1954, made by the Industrial Tribunal, Delhi, directing the appellant (Punjab National Bank) to pay travelling and halting allowances to the representatives of various Unions (other than the two located in Delhi) to attend the hearing before the Tribunal in Delhi.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Punjab National Bank) moved the Punjab High Court for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of the Industrial Tribunal. The Punjab High Court dismissed the petition in limine (i.e., without a full hearing) on May 14, 1954.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (Punjab National Bank) obtained special leave from the Supreme Court on October 18, 1954, to appeal the decision of the Punjab High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether an Industrial Tribunal, in the exercise of its discretion under Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, has the power to direct one party to pay the travelling and halting allowances of the other party's representatives in a pending proceeding, irrespective of the final outcome.

facts: During an ongoing dispute adjudication between a bank and its workmen, the workmen's unions applied to the Industrial Tribunal for an order.
The unions requested that the bank be directed to pay the travelling and halting allowances for their representatives to attend the hearings in Delhi.
The Tribunal granted the order, not based on a specific provision of law, but on what it claimed was the "general practice" of Industrial Courts.
The bank appealed this order to the Supreme Court, arguing that the Tribunal had acted without jurisdiction.
law: The case centered on the interpretation of Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which grants an Industrial Tribunal discretion over the "costs of, and incidental to, any proceeding."
The Supreme Court clarified that the discretion granted under this section is a *judicial discretion*.
This means it must be exercised according to the rules of reason and justice, not based on caprice, private opinion, or "some fanciful idea of benevolence or sympathy."
application: The Court first addressed the Tribunal's reliance on "general practice." It found that there was no uniform or consistent practice in this matter, and even if such a practice existed, it was not warranted by law or the principles of justice.

The Court then interpreted Section 11(7) and held that a proper construction of the law does not give a Tribunal the power to order one party to pay the costs of another party *in advance* and *irrespective of the final result* of the case.

The Court explicitly disapproved of a previous decision (*Certain Banking Companies v. Their Workmen*) that had justified such orders on grounds like the employer's superior financial resources or principles of natural justice, deeming these reasons unsustainable in law.

Instead, the Court approved the reasoning in another case (*Jeevan Textile Mills*), which stated that orders for costs must be made on "well-recognised principles" and not on abstract ideas of what seems desirable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Industrial Tribunal's order was without jurisdiction. It held that the power to award costs under Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act does not include the authority to direct one party to pay the travel and halting allowances of the other party's representatives during a pending proceeding, irrespective of the final outcome.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an Industrial Tribunal, in the exercise of its discretion under Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, has the power to direct one party to pay the travelling and halting allowances of the other party's representatives in a pending proceeding, irrespective of the final outcome.
appellant_arguments: The order to pay travelling and halting allowances in a pending proceeding is wholly without jurisdiction.
The expression 'costs of any proceeding' in Section 11(7) refers to the costs of the entire proceeding as determined at its conclusion, not costs to be incurred in the future by a party.
The expression 'costs incidental to any proceeding' refers to costs of concluded interlocutory applications, not future expenses.

Neither of the expressions 'costs of any proceeding' nor 'costs incidental to any proceeding' includes costs payable in advance or future halting and travelling allowances for a party to attend the hearing.
respondent_arguments: The concluding portion of Section 11(7) shows that costs can be granted in advance during a pending proceeding.
An Industrial Tribunal becomes functus officio after submitting its award.
Since an application for recovery of costs must be made to the Tribunal ('it'), it must be done before the Tribunal becomes functus officio, meaning while the proceeding is still pending.
The order was justified based on the general practice of Industrial Courts, particularly in cases involving banks.

cases.case_name: Jeevan Textile Mills, Hyderabad (Deccan) v. Their Workmen
cases.principle: The discretion given to a Tribunal under s. 11 (7) of the Industrial Disputes Act is a judicial discretion and must be exercised according to the rules of reason and justice, not by chance or caprice or private opinion or some fanciful idea of benevolence or sympathy.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An Industrial Tribunal, exercising its discretion under section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, has no power to direct a party to pay the costs of another party in advance during a pending proceeding, irrespective of the final result. The expressions "costs of any proceeding" and "costs incidental to any proceeding" refer to costs determined at the conclusion of the proceeding or application, not costs to be incurred in the future.
obiter: The discretion granted to a Tribunal to award costs is a judicial discretion that must be exercised according to the rules of reason and justice, not based on caprice, private opinion, or sympathy.
The general rule is that costs follow the event unless the Court, for good reasons, orders otherwise.

The relative financial resources of the parties is not a valid ground for ordering the richer party to pay the expenses of the weaker party in advance and irrespective of the ultimate result of the dispute.
'Social justice' does not mean that reason and fairness must always yield to the convenience of one party at the cost of the other in an adjudication proceeding.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On a plain reading of Section 11(7) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Tribunal has no power to direct the payment of costs in advance by one party to another in a pending proceeding, irrespective of the final result. The expression 'costs of any proceeding' means the costs of the entire proceeding as determined at its conclusion, not costs to be incurred in the future. Similarly, 'costs incidental to any proceeding' refers to costs of concluded interlocutory applications. The respondent's argument that an application for costs must be made to the Tribunal ('it') before it becomes functus officio is fallacious, as the expression 'it' in the concluding portion of the sub-section refers to the appropriate Government and not to the Tribunal.
legal_tests_applied: The discretion granted to a Tribunal under Section 11(7) is a judicial discretion and must be exercised according to the rules of reason and justice, not by chance, caprice, private opinion, or some fanciful idea of benevolence or sympathy.
Statutory interpretation of the phrases 'costs of any proceeding' and 'costs incidental to any proceeding' by their plain meaning and in comparison to Section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
policy_considerations: The general rule is that costs follow the event unless the Court, for good reasons, otherwise orders. It is a negation of justice and reason to direct one party to pay in advance the costs of the other irrespective of the final result.
The concept of 'social justice' does not mean that reason and fairness must always yield to the convenience of one party at the cost of the other, as such a one-sided view is akin to caprice.

Making a richer party pay the expenses of a weaker party, irrespective of the merits, would encourage frivolous and unsubstantial disputes, which runs counter to the Act's purpose of promoting industrial peace.
The fact that a party has superior financial resources cannot be a ground for making them pay for the expenses of the other party.
The compulsory nature of adjudication applies equally to both parties and cannot be a reason to impose a penalty on one party and not the other.

The principles of natural justice cannot be invoked to support an order that penalises one party by making it pay for the costs of the other party in advance, irrespective of the result; such an order is neither natural nor has any element of justice in it.
